A mortal enemy is a person, group, or force that is in deep, total, and unrelenting opposition to you — one whose hostility toward you is so extreme that it is considered permanent and absolute. It is not just someone who dislikes you or disagrees with you. It is someone whose very existence is in direct and irreconcilable conflict with yours.

The plural form is mortal enemies.
Breaking It Down Word by Word

To truly understand the phrase, it helps to understand the job each word is doing.

"Enemy" means someone who is actively against you — someone who wishes you harm, works to defeat you, or stands in opposition to you. An enemy is not a stranger who ignores you. An enemy is someone who is against you.

"Mortal" in this phrase is an adjective that intensifies the word "enemy" to the highest possible degree. It carries two powerful meanings at once:

  • "To the death" — the conflict is so serious it could end in destruction or ruin.
  • "Absolute and total" — the hatred or opposition is complete, not partial. There is no middle ground, no possibility of peace, and no soft edges.

Together, mortal enemy means an enemy of the most extreme, permanent, and deadly kind.
What Makes Someone a Mortal Enemy (and Not Just an Enemy)?

Think of it like a scale of opposition:

Rival → Opponent → Enemy → Mortal Enemy

Each step is more serious than the last. Here is how they differ:

  • A rival competes with you but may respect you and there is no deep hatred.
  • An opponent disagrees with you or works against you in a specific context.
  • An enemy actively wishes you harm or works to defeat you.
  • A mortal enemy does all of that — but with total commitment, deep hatred, and permanence. The conflict between you is not a temporary argument. It is a defining feature of both your lives.

A mortal enemy is not just someone you fight with today. It is someone whose opposition to you feels like it will never end, and can never be resolved through compromise or forgiveness.

The phrase is used in two ways — literally and figuratively.

Literally, a mortal enemy is someone who genuinely wants to destroy you, defeat you entirely, or cause your death. This is how it is used in wars, historical rivalries, and serious conflicts where lives are at stake.

Example: "For centuries, the two kingdoms were mortal enemies — they fought to wipe each other off the map."

Figuratively (and this is far more common in everyday language), a mortal enemy is someone whose opposition to you is simply the most extreme and absolute it can be — even if no one is actually being killed. The word "mortal" is being used to express intensity, not necessarily physical danger.

Example: "Those two companies are mortal enemies. They will do absolutely anything to destroy each other in the marketplace."

Example: "She and her sister used to be mortal enemies as teenagers, but now they get along fine." (Here it is used with slight humor or exaggeration to mean they intensely disliked each other.)
Key Characteristics of a Mortal Enemy

Whenever you see or use this phrase, these qualities are almost always implied:

  1. Deep, intense hatred or opposition — not mild dislike, but something burning and profound.
  2. Permanence — this is not a temporary falling-out. The enmity is seen as long-lasting, possibly lifelong.
  3. Irreconcilability — there is no expected resolution. Peace between mortal enemies feels impossible.
  4. Totality — the opposition covers everything. It is not conflict in one specific area; it is a complete and all-encompassing clash.
  5. High stakes — something important is at risk: power, survival, beliefs, identity, or dominance.

Yes. One person can consider another their mortal enemy even if the feeling is not perfectly mutual. However, in most uses of the phrase, the enmity is understood to be mutual — both sides deeply oppose each other.
Real-World Examples to Cement the Idea

• In history: Two rival empires who fought across centuries to destroy each other's power and dominance were mortal enemies.
  • In fiction: Classic storytelling is full of mortal enemies — a hero and a villain who are locked in an endless, defining struggle. Think of any great superhero and their greatest villain.
  • In nature: Prey and predator species are sometimes poetically called mortal enemies because their relationship is one of survival — one lives, the other dies.
  • In everyday life (figurative): Two neighbors who have been in bitter, unresolved conflict for decades, each trying to make the other's life miserable, might jokingly or seriously be called each other's mortal enemies.
  • In politics or ideology: Two groups who hold completely opposite beliefs and see each other as a fundamental threat to their way of life are often described as mortal enemies.

• A mortal enemy is not just someone you are annoyed with or had a bad experience with.
  • A mortal enemy is not a temporary rival you might one day reconcile with (though in fiction, former mortal enemies sometimes do reconcile — which is always treated as a dramatic, remarkable event).
  • A mortal enemy is not a casual competitor. The word "mortal" lifts the phrase far above ordinary competition.
The Emotional Weight of the Phrase

When someone calls another person their "mortal enemy," it signals something heavy and serious. It tells you that this is not just conflict — it is the defining conflict. It says: "This person and I are fundamentally opposed, and that will not change."

Even when used with humor or exaggeration in everyday speech (like saying "broccoli is my mortal enemy"), the phrase works because everyone understands it means total, absolute, and unrelenting opposition — which is exactly what makes it powerful, dramatic, and vivid.
